claim: CCL2 is induced by HIV-1 clade B (HIV-1B) infection of macrophages.
source: We found that CCL2 induced by HIV-1 clade B (HIV-1B) infection of macrophages enhanced virus production, while CCL2 immuno-depletion reversed this effect.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCL2 induced by HIV-1B infection of macrophages enhanced virus production.
source: We found that CCL2 induced by HIV-1 clade B (HIV-1B) infection of macrophages enhanced virus production, while CCL2 immuno-depletion reversed this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing increased virus production with CCL2 treatment.

claim: CCL2 immuno-depletion reversed the enhancement of virus production by HIV-1B.
source: We found that CCL2 induced by HIV-1 clade B (HIV-1B) infection of macrophages enhanced virus production, while CCL2 immuno-depletion reversed this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing decreased virus production with α-CCL2 treatment.

claim: HIV-1 clade C (HIV-1C) was refractory to CCL2 levels.
source: Additionally, HIV-1 clade C (HIV-1C) was refractory to CCL2 levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing no change in virus production with CCL2 modulation.

claim: CCL2-mediated increase in virus production requires Gag late motif LYPX present in HIV-1B.
source: We show that CCL2-mediated increase in virus production requires Gag late motif LYPX present in HIV-1B, but absent in HIV-1C, and ALIX protein that recruits ESCRT III complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing that deletion of LY motif eliminates CCL2-responsiveness.

claim: The LYPX motif is absent in HIV-1C.
source: We show that CCL2-mediated increase in virus production requires Gag late motif LYPX present in HIV-1B, but absent in HIV-1C, and ALIX protein that recruits ESCRT III complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data in Figure 3A and 3B showing LY deletion in HIV-1C isolates.

claim: CCL2-mediated increase in virus production requires ALIX protein that recruits ESCRT III complex.
source: We show that CCL2-mediated increase in virus production requires Gag late motif LYPX present in HIV-1B, but absent in HIV-1C, and ALIX protein that recruits ESCRT III complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4E showing loss of CCL2-responsiveness in ALIX knockdown cells.

claim: CCL2 immuno-depletion sequestered ALIX to F-actin structures.
source: CCL2 immuno-depletion sequestered ALIX to F-actin structures, while CCL2 addition mobilized it to cytoplasm facilitating Gag-ALIX binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 6 and Figure 7 showing colocalization of ALIX with F-actin upon α-CCL2 treatment.

claim: CCL2 addition mobilized ALIX to cytoplasm facilitating Gag-ALIX binding.
source: CCL2 immuno-depletion sequestered ALIX to F-actin structures, while CCL2 addition mobilized it to cytoplasm facilitating Gag-ALIX binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 6 and Figure 7, and GST pull-down data in Figure 5C showing increased ALIX-Gag binding with CCL2 treatment.

claim: The LYPX motif improves virus replication.
source: The LYPX motif improves virus replication and its absence renders the virus less fit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 10 showing increased replication of HIV-1C+LY compared to HIV-1C wild type.

claim: The absence of LYPX motif renders the virus less fit.
source: The LYPX motif improves virus replication and its absence renders the virus less fit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 10 showing reduced replication of HIV-1C compared to HIV-1B.

claim: Novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred ALIX binding.
source: Interestingly, novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred ALIX binding, CCL2-responsiveness and enhanced virus replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down data in Figure 11A showing ALIX binding to HIV-1C p6 with PYRE or PYKE insertions.

claim: Novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred CCL2-responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred ALIX binding, CCL2-responsiveness and enhanced virus replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 13 showing CCL2-responsiveness of HIV-1C+PYRE and HIV-1C+PYKE viruses.

claim: Novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred enhanced virus replication.
source: Interestingly, novel variants of HIV-1C with PYRE/PYKE tetrapeptide insertions in Gag-p6 conferred ALIX binding, CCL2-responsiveness and enhanced virus replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 11B showing increased replication of HIV-1C+PYRE and HIV-1C+PYKE compared to HIV-1C wild type.

claim: Cellular ESCRT machinery plays pivotal role in HIV-1 budding and release.
source: Cellular ESCRT machinery plays pivotal role in HIV-1 budding and release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on ESCRT function in HIV-1 budding.

claim: HIV-1 Gag polyprotein includes two motifs in the C-terminal p6 - late motif I (PTAP) and late motif II (LYPX).
source: HIV-1 Gag polyprotein includes two motifs in the C-terminal p6 - late motif I (PTAP) and late motif II (LYPX) - which recruit host proteins TSG-101 (Pornillos et al., 2002; VerPlank et al., 2001) and ALIX (Usami et al., 2007; Fisher et al., 2007; Munshi et al., 2007), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and is consistent with known HIV-1 Gag structure.

claim: PTAP motif recruits host protein TSG-101.
source: HIV-1 Gag polyprotein includes two motifs in the C-terminal p6 - late motif I (PTAP) and late motif II (LYPX) - which recruit host proteins TSG-101 (Pornillos et al., 2002; VerPlank et al., 2001) and ALIX (Usami et al., 2007; Fisher et al., 2007; Munshi et al., 2007), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: LYPX motif recruits host protein ALIX.
source: HIV-1 Gag polyprotein includes two motifs in the C-terminal p6 - late motif I (PTAP) and late motif II (LYPX) - which recruit host proteins TSG-101 (Pornillos et al., 2002; VerPlank et al., 2001) and ALIX (Usami et al., 2007; Fisher et al., 2007; Munshi et al., 2007), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and experimental data in Figure 3C and Figure 5C.

claim: TSG101 is a subunit of the cellular ESCRT-I complex.
source: TSG101 is a subunit of the cellular ESCRT-I complex and ALIX is an accessory protein of ESCRT-III complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of ESCRT complex composition.

claim: ALIX is an accessory protein of ESCRT-III complex.
source: TSG101 is a subunit of the cellular ESCRT-I complex and ALIX is an accessory protein of ESCRT-III complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of ESCRT complex composition.

claim: TSG101 and ALIX physically link late domains I and II of HIV-1 Gag-p6 to ESCRT I and ESCRT-III complexes, respectively.
source: These two proteins physically link late domains I and II of HIV-1 Gag-p6 to ESCRT I and ESCRT-III complexes, respectively (Sun et al., 2015) (Strack et al., 2003) and are both essential for membrane fission steps like MVB biogenesis, cytokinesis and virus budding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: TSG101 and ALIX are both essential for membrane fission steps like MVB biogenesis, cytokinesis and virus budding.
source: These two proteins physically link late domains I and II of HIV-1 Gag-p6 to ESCRT I and ESCRT-III complexes, respectively (Sun et al., 2015) (Strack et al., 2003) and are both essential for membrane fission steps like MVB biogenesis, cytokinesis and virus budding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: CCL2 is a potent β-chemokine induced upon HIV-1 infection of primary human macrophages.
source: CCL2 is a potent β-chemokine induced upon HIV-1 infection of primary human macrophages (Mengozzi et al., 1999), as a host innate immune response designed to attract monocytes and T lymphocytes to trigger inflammation against the pathogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: CCL2 is a host innate immune response designed to attract monocytes and T lymphocytes to trigger inflammation against the pathogen.
source: CCL2 is a potent β-chemokine induced upon HIV-1 infection of primary human macrophages (Mengozzi et al., 1999), as a host innate immune response designed to attract monocytes and T lymphocytes to trigger inflammation against the pathogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of CCL2 function in immune response.

claim: CCL2 mRNA is elevated in both macrophages and PBMCs upon HIV-1 infection.
source: CCL2 mRNA is elevated in both macrophages and PBMCs upon HIV-1 infection (Mengozzi et al., 1999; Vázquez et al., 2005; Wetzel et al., 2002; Woelk et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Plasma levels of CCL2 strongly correlate with plasma viral loads in HIV-infected individuals.
source: Furthermore, plasma levels of CCL2 strongly correlate with plasma viral loads in HIV-infected individuals (Weiss et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: CCL2 upregulation and elevated CCL2 protein levels were found to be specifically associated with viremic patients.
source: In a thorough analysis of a large number of host proinflammatory genes to identify markers that correlate with HIV-1 viral loads, CCL2 upregulation and elevated CCL2 protein levels were found to be specifically associated with viremic patients (Ansari et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: CCL2 addition enhances HIV-1 replication in cultured CD4+ T cells.
source: CCL2 addition enhances HIV-1 replication in cultured CD4+ T cells (Kinter et al., 1998) and in macrophages (Fantuzzi et al., 2003), neutralization of CCL2 inhibits virus release and leads to intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag (Fantuzzi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: CCL2 addition enhances HIV-1 replication in macrophages.
source: CCL2 addition enhances HIV-1 replication in cultured CD4+ T cells (Kinter et al., 1998) and in macrophages (Fantuzzi et al., 2003), neutralization of CCL2 inhibits virus release and leads to intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag (Fantuzzi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Neutralization of CCL2 inhibits virus release and leads to intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag.
source: CCL2 addition enhances HIV-1 replication in cultured CD4+ T cells (Kinter et al., 1998) and in macrophages (Fantuzzi et al., 2003), neutralization of CCL2 inhibits virus release and leads to intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag (Fantuzzi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and experimental data in Figure 1C.

claim: Infection of macrophages with clade C HIV-1 (HIV-1C), unlike that of HIV-1B, is not associated with a robust CCL2 induction.
source: It is intriguing to note that infection of macrophages with clade C HIV-1 (HIV-1C), unlike that of HIV-1B, is not associated with a robust CCL2 induction (Campbell et al., 2007; Rao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Addition of CCL2 resulted in mobilization of ALIX associated with F-actin to the cytoplasm making it available to bind HIV-1 Gag-p6.
source: In this report, we show that addition of CCL2 resulted in mobilization of ALIX associated with F-actin to the cytoplasm making it available to bind HIV-1 Gag-p6, which consequently enhanced virion release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5, Figure 6, and Figure 7.

claim: Mobilization of ALIX to the cytoplasm by CCL2 consequently enhanced virion release.
source: In this report, we show that addition of CCL2 resulted in mobilization of ALIX associated with F-actin to the cytoplasm making it available to bind HIV-1 Gag-p6, which consequently enhanced virion release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1, Figure 4, and Figure 5.

claim: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a dramatic colocalization of ALIX with F-actin structures.
source: Furthermore, we found that immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a dramatic colocalization of ALIX with F-actin structures, which was associated with decrease of virion release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: Colocalization of ALIX with F-actin structures was associated with decrease of virion release.
source: Furthermore, we found that immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a dramatic colocalization of ALIX with F-actin structures, which was associated with decrease of virion release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The inability of HIV-1C to exploit the increased availability of ALIX is due to a lack of the LY dipeptide in late domain II or LYPX motif, in its Gag-p6.
source: On the contrary, we found that HIV-1C is refractory to CCL2 levels and that the inability to exploit the increased availability of ALIX is due to a lack of the LY dipeptide in late domain II or LYPX motif, in it's Gag-p6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3, Figure 4, and Figure 5.

claim: HIV-1C is known to be less fit than HIV-1B or other group M HIV-1 viruses.
source: HIV-1C is known to be less fit than HIV-1B or other group M HIV-1 viruses (Ariën et al., 2005; Ariën et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and experimental data in Figure 10.

claim: The basis for reduced fitness of HIV-1C has been reported to be inefficient virus entry due to its Env gene.
source: While the basis for this reduced fitness has been reported to be inefficient virus entry due to its Env gene (Ball et al., 2003), there is increasing evidence that a late event such as virus release may also be inefficient.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The absence of LY dipeptide is responsible for the reduced replication fitness of HIV-1C.
source: For example, comparative study of a large number of HIV-1C and HIV-1B isolates has concluded that the absence of LY dipeptide is responsible for the reduced replication fitness of HIV-1C (Kiguoya et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and experimental data in Figure 10.

claim: Variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display ALIX binding to Gag-p6.
source: We report here that variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display ALIX binding to Gag-p6, enhanced virion release, CCL2-responsiveness and improved replication capacity of such viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 11A.

claim: Variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display enhanced virion release.
source: We report here that variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display ALIX binding to Gag-p6, enhanced virion release, CCL2-responsiveness and improved replication capacity of such viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 11C.

claim: Variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display improved replication capacity.
source: We report here that variants of HIV-1C that acquire novel late domain II-like, tetrapeptide insertions display ALIX binding to Gag-p6, enhanced virion release, CCL2-responsiveness and improved replication capacity of such viruses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 11B.

claim: CCL2 leads to redistribution of ALIX.
source: Our finding that CCL2 leads to redistribution of ALIX can have wide-ranging relevance to many other viruses and potentially in MVB and exosome biogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and Figure 7.

claim: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a significant reduction (~10 fold) in the replication of HIV-1BADA.
source: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a significant reduction (~10 fold) in the replication of HIV-1BADA (Figure 1A), accompanied by a corresponding increase in the intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag precursor (pr55: Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag precursor (pr55) in HIV-1BADA-infected MDMs.
source: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 led to a significant reduction (~10 fold) in the replication of HIV-1BADA (Figure 1A), accompanied by a corresponding increase in the intracellular accumulation of HIV-1 Gag precursor (pr55: Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Immuno-depletion of CCL2 in HIV-1IndieC1-infected MDMs neither inhibited virus replication nor increased intracellular Gag levels.
source: In contrast, immuno-depletion of CCL2 in HIV-1IndieC1-infected MDMs neither inhibited virus replication nor increased intracellular Gag levels (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Virion release of HIV-1BADA, but not HIV-1CIndieC1, is severely reduced upon CCL2 immuno-depletion.
source: Comparison of relative amounts of p24 released into the culture medium as virus particles to intracellular levels of Gag suggested that virion release of HIV-1BADA, but not HIV-1CIndieC1, is severely reduced upon CCL2 immuno-depletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Addition of CCL2 to the HIV-1BADA-infected macrophage cultures enhanced virus replication.
source: Furthermore, addition of CCL2 to the HIV-1BADA-infected macrophage cultures enhanced virus replication, while HIV-1IndieC–infected cells were unaffected (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HIV-1IndieC–infected cells were unaffected by addition of CCL2.
source: Furthermore, addition of CCL2 to the HIV-1BADA-infected macrophage cultures enhanced virus replication, while HIV-1IndieC–infected cells were unaffected (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CCL2-mediated stimulation of HIV-1 replication (~50% increase) was also observed in CEM-CCR5, a CD4+ T-cell-derived cell line.
source: The CCL2-mediated stimulation of HIV-1 replication (~50% increase) was also observed in CEM-CCR5, a CD4+ T-cell-derived cell line (Figure 2) but the α-CCL2 suppression of virus production was minimal (~25%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The α-CCL2 suppression of virus production in CEM-CCR5 was minimal (~25%).
source: The CCL2-mediated stimulation of HIV-1 replication (~50% increase) was also observed in CEM-CCR5, a CD4+ T-cell-derived cell line (Figure 2) but the α-CCL2 suppression of virus production was minimal (~25%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Particle release of HIV-1B, but not HIV-1C, was affected by modulating CCL2 levels in the medium.
source: Together, our results indicated that particle release of HIV-1B, but not HIV-1C, was affected by modulating CCL2 levels in the medium.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: The inhibition of virus replication by immune-depletion of CCL2 in CEM-CCR5 cells was much milder than in macrophages.
source: However, it appeared that the inhibition of virus replication by immune-depletion of CCL2 in CEM-CCR5 cells was much milder than in macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Robust levels of CCR2 mRNA and protein were detected in MDMs, CEM-CCR5 cells, and HeLa cells.
source: Our results indicated that robust levels of CCR2 mRNA and protein were detected in all three cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CCL2 production in both MDMs and HeLa cells was significant.
source: CCL2 production in both MDMs and HeLa cells was significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and D), but the levels of CCL2 produced in CEM-CCR5 cells was below the level of detection – and we only detected miniscule amounts upon HIV infection or robustly only in samples where CCL2 was extraneously added (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and D.

claim: The levels of CCL2 produced in CEM-CCR5 cells was below the level of detection.
source: CCL2 production in both MDMs and HeLa cells was significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and D), but the levels of CCL2 produced in CEM-CCR5 cells was below the level of detection – and we only detected miniscule amounts upon HIV infection or robustly only in samples where CCL2 was extraneously added (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The limiting amounts of CCL2 is primarily responsible for the minimal inhibition in virus replication observed upon the addition of α-CCL2 in CEM-CCR5 cells.
source: These data suggest that the limiting amounts of CCL2 is primarily responsible for the minimal inhibition in virus replication observed upon the addition of α-CCL2 in this CD4 T cell line.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2.

claim: CCL2-mediated enhancement of virus production was observed in both macrophages and T cells.
source: Nevertheless, CCL2-mediated enhancement of virus production (conversely, inhibition of virus production by CCL2 depletion) was observed in both macrophages and T cells, indicating that this effect is not limited to macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: CCR2 is present on both CD4 T cells and macrophages.
source: Importantly, CCR2 is present on both CD4 T cells and macrophages, suggesting that both can respond to the presence of CCL2 by increasing virus replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both CD4 T cells and macrophages can respond to the presence of CCL2 by increasing virus replication.
source: Importantly, CCR2 is present on both CD4 T cells and macrophages, suggesting that both can respond to the presence of CCL2 by increasing virus replication.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing CCR2 expression and CCL2-responsiveness in both cell types.

claim: CCL2 addition can reverse the effects of CCL2 immuno-depletion on HIV-1BADA replication.
source: Our results showed that while the virus replication was inhibited until day 9, it resumed at day 9 and reached peak virion production at day 18 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: HIV-1B viruses contain an LYPX motif in addition to PTAP motif.
source: It has been reported that HIV-1C isolates contain a LY dipeptide deletion in the Gag-p6 LYPX motif, whereas all non-HIV-1C isolates examined retain an intact LYPX motif (Patil and Bhattacharya, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and sequence analysis data in Figure 3A.

claim: HIV-1C isolates contain a LY dipeptide deletion in the Gag-p6 LYPX motif.
source: It has been reported that HIV-1C isolates contain a LY dipeptide deletion in the Gag-p6 LYPX motif, whereas all non-HIV-1C isolates examined retain an intact LYPX motif (Patil and Bhattacharya, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature and sequence analysis data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: While LYPX motif was conserved in clade B sequences, it was not conserved in clade C sequences, mainly due to a LY dipeptide deletion.
source: Our HIV-1B vs. HIV-1C alignment shows that while LYPX motif was conserved in clade B sequences, it was not conserved in clade C sequences, mainly due to a LY dipeptide deletion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The tyrosine 36 (Y36) residue in the late motif II (LYPX) of Gag is critical for binding to the conserved F676 in the flexible 'V' domain of ALIX.
source: Previous studies have revealed that the tyrosine 36 (Y36) residue in the late motif II (LYPX) of Gag is critical for binding to the conserved F676 in the flexible 'V' domain of ALIX (Fisher et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Y36 residue is conserved in about 96% of clade B isolates examined.
source: Our analysis of 695 clade B and 475 clade C isolates showed that while the Y36 residue is conserved in about 96% of clade B isolates examined, it was absent in >99% of clade C isolates examined (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Y36 residue was absent in >99% of clade C isolates examined.
source: Our analysis of 695 clade B and 475 clade C isolates showed that while the Y36 residue is conserved in about 96% of clade B isolates examined, it was absent in >99% of clade C isolates examined (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The PTAP motif was fully conserved in both B and C isolates.
source: On the other hand, the PTAP motif was fully conserved in both B and C isolates.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis data in Figure 3A.

claim: HIV-1B, but not HIV-1C Gag-p6 bound to ALIX.
source: Our results indicated that HIV-1B, but not HIV-1C Gag-p6 bound to ALIX (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CCL2-responsiveness was dependent on the presence of LYPX, and not on the PTAP motif.
source: Since the two clades differ in the presence or absence of LYPX motif in Gag-p6 (Figure 3, Figure 4A), and since our results demonstrated that CCL2 differentially influences virus replication of the two clades (Figure 1, Figure 2), we surmised that CCL2-mediated virus release was dependent on the LYPX, and not on the PTAP motif.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3, and Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of the PTAP motif drastically reduced (by ~75%) virus production.
source: We found that deletion of the PTAP motif drastically reduced (by ~75%) virus production (reflecting the well-known major role of the PTAP motif in virus budding).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: HIV-1BADA-PTAP(+LIRL) showed CCL2 responsiveness.
source: Interestingly, even though the virus production was significantly reduced due to the absence of PTAP, HIV-1BADA-PTAP(+LIRL) showed CCL2 responsiveness (Figure 4B, -PTAP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of the LY dipeptide (ΔLY mutation) in HIV-1B showed a less severe reduction in virus production.
source: Deletion of the LY dipeptide (ΔLY mutation) in HIV-1B showed a less severe reduction in virus production, reflecting the auxiliary role of the LYPX motif (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LY deletion in HIV-1B completely eliminated the CCL2-responsiveness.
source: Importantly, LY deletion in HIV-1B completely eliminated the CCL2-responsiveness as neither the addition nor depletion of CCL2 had any effect on virus production of HIV-1BADAΔLY (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The pattern of virus production of HIV-1BADAΔLY was identical to that of wild-type HIV-1CIndieC1 in all three conditions.
source: In fact, the pattern of virus production of HIV-1BADAΔLY was identical to that of wild-type HIV-1CIndieC1 in all three conditions (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: When both PTAP and LYPX motifs were absent, virus production was completely abrogated.
source: When both motifs were absent, virus production was completely abrogated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The insertion of the LY dipeptide (HIV-1CIndieC1+LY) rendered HIV-1CIndieC1 responsive to the presence or absence of CCL2.
source: We found that the insertion of the LY dipeptide (HIV-1CIndieC1+LY) rendered HIV-1CIndieC1 responsive to the presence or absence of CCL2 and yielded a pattern of viral production that recapitulated the wild-type HIV-1BADA (Figure 4C) irrespective of whether or not there was an intact PTAP motif (HIV-1CIndieC1+LY and HIV-1CIndieC1-PTAP (+LIRL), +LY).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Wild-type HIV-1IndieC1, which lacks a LYPX motif, was insensitive to changes in CCL2 levels in the medium.
source: Furthermore, wild-type virus, which lacks a LYPX motif (HIV-1IndieC1) was insensitive to changes in CCL2 levels in the medium.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: A decrease in extracellular p24 was associated with a corresponding intracellular increase in Pr55 Gag levels, specifically in a manner dependent on the presence of LYPX motif.
source: Our results indicated that a decrease in extracellular p24 was associated with a corresponding intracellular increase in Pr55 Gag levels, specifically in a manner dependent on the presence of LYPX motif (see α-CCL2 conditions for HIV-1B WT and HIV-1C+LY, HIV-1C-PTAP, +LY), establishing that the inhibition of particle production was not due to an inherent decrease in intracellular Gag, but rather due to an assembly and/or particle release step defect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibition of particle production was not due to an inherent decrease in intracellular Gag, but rather due to an assembly and/or particle release step defect.
source: Our results indicated that a decrease in extracellular p24 was associated with a corresponding intracellular increase in Pr55 Gag levels, specifically in a manner dependent on the presence of LYPX motif (see α-CCL2 conditions for HIV-1B WT and HIV-1C+LY, HIV-1C-PTAP, +LY), establishing that the inhibition of particle production was not due to an inherent decrease in intracellular Gag, but rather due to an assembly and/or particle release step defect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCL2 had no effect on the infectivity of the viruses.
source: However, we did not see any effect of CCL2 addition or depletion on the infectivity of the viruses, suggesting that the CCL2-dependency manifests at the late events but not at the early events (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CCL2-dependency manifests at the late events but not at the early events.
source: However, we did not see any effect of CCL2 addition or depletion on the infectivity of the viruses, suggesting that the CCL2-dependency manifests at the late events but not at the early events (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Viruses that harbored an LYPX motif responded to CCL2 modulation.
source: In summary, measurement of virus production under various treatments indicated that viruses that harbored an LYPX motif (HIV-1ADA WT, HIV-1ADA-PTAP (+LIRL), HIV-1CIndieC1+LY and HIV-1CIndieC1-PTAP +LY) responded to CCL2 modulation and viruses that lacked the LYPX motif (HIV-1ADAPTAP, ΔLY and HIV-1CIndieC1 WT), irrespective of the presence or absence of PTAP, were non-responsive to CCL2 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Viruses that lacked the LYPX motif, irrespective of the presence or absence of PTAP, were non-responsive to CCL2.
source: In summary, measurement of virus production under various treatments indicated that viruses that harbored an LYPX motif (HIV-1ADA WT, HIV-1ADA-PTAP (+LIRL), HIV-1CIndieC1+LY and HIV-1CIndieC1-PTAP +LY) responded to CCL2 modulation and viruses that lacked the LYPX motif (HIV-1ADAPTAP, ΔLY and HIV-1CIndieC1 WT), irrespective of the presence or absence of PTAP, were non-responsive to CCL2 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The knock-down of ALIX resulted in a > 95% decrease in cellular ALIX protein.
source: Immunoblot analysis indicated that the knock-down resulted in a > 95% decrease in cellular ALIX protein (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Virus production was reduced by about threefold in ALIX knockdown cells.
source: Virus production was reduced by about threefold in ALIX knockdown cells and was not further influenced by the presence or absence of CCL2 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Virus production in ALIX knockdown cells was not further influenced by the presence or absence of CCL2.
source: Virus production was reduced by about threefold in ALIX knockdown cells and was not further influenced by the presence or absence of CCL2 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The responsiveness to CCL2 requires LYPX motif in the virus and the presence of ALIX in the cell.
source: These results collectively established that the responsiveness to CCL2 requires LYPX motif in the virus and the presence of ALIX in the cell.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: ALIX mRNA levels remained unaltered in the presence or absence of CCL2 or α-CCL2.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of mRNA in HeLa cells over multiple time points indicated that ALIX mRNA levels remained unaltered in the presence or absence of CCL2 or α-CCL2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Total ALIX levels remained the same with all the treatments (untreated, CCL2-treated and α-CCL2-treated).
source: As shown in Figure 5B, total ALIX levels remained the same with all the treatments, consistent with the qRT-PCR results (Figure 5B top panel of immunoblots and the corresponding graph – blue bars - to the right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The level of soluble ALIX in untreated or CCL2-treated cells was higher than in α-CCL2-treated cells.
source: However, the level of soluble ALIX in untreated or CCL2-treated cells was higher than in α-CCL2-treated cells (Figure 5B – middle panel: 4 hr treatment; compare lanes 1 and 2 to 3, UT and CCL2 to α-CCL2, and the corresponding bar graphs, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was very little insoluble ALIX (Pellet 2) with CCL2-treatment.
source: There was very little insoluble ALIX (Pellet 2) with CCL2-treatment (Figure 5B, bottom panel, lane 2), whereas increased ALIX was detected in the insoluble fraction upon α-CCL2 treatment (Figure 5B, bottom panel, lane 3 – see corresponding bar graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increased ALIX was detected in the insoluble fraction upon α-CCL2 treatment.
source: There was very little insoluble ALIX (Pellet 2) with CCL2-treatment (Figure 5B, bottom panel, lane 2), whereas increased ALIX was detected in the insoluble fraction upon α-CCL2 treatment (Figure 5B, bottom panel, lane 3 – see corresponding bar graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Soluble ALIX was increased by CCL2.
source: These results indicated that while total cellular ALIX remained the same under all three conditions (top row, lanes 1 to 4), soluble ALIX was increased by CCL2 (middle row, lane 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B.

claim: GST-Bp6 bound to more ALIX when CCL2 was added to the medium.
source: GST-Bp6 bound to more ALIX when CCL2 was added to the medium, which was consistent with an increase in soluble ALIX in the cells (Figure 5C, compare lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Under conditions where CCL2 was depleted (α-CCL2), no association between GST-Bp6 and ALIX was detected.
source: However, under conditions where CCL2 was depleted (α-CCL2), no association was detected (Figure 5C, compare lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ALIX did not bind GST-Cp6 under any condition.
source: As expected, ALIX did not bind GST-Cp6 under any condition (Figure 5C, lanes 7–9) despite the presence of robust levels of ALIX in the soluble fraction (Figure 5C, input).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Unlike ALIX, p6-binding to TSG101 was not affected by changing CCL2 levels.
source: We found that unlike ALIX, p6-binding to TSG101 was not affected by changing CCL2 levels (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both GagB-p6 and GagC-p6 proteins bound to TSG101 in all cases.
source: Both GagB-p6 and GagC-p6 proteins bound to TSG101 in all cases, suggesting that responsiveness to CCL2 is specifically correlated to ALIX-binding but not TSG101-binding (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Responsiveness to CCL2 is specifically correlated to ALIX-binding but not TSG101-binding.
source: Both GagB-p6 and GagC-p6 proteins bound to TSG101 in all cases, suggesting that responsiveness to CCL2 is specifically correlated to ALIX-binding but not TSG101-binding (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Intracellular Gag-p6-ALIX binding is dependent on the presence of the LYPX motif in Gag-p6.
source: These results indicate that: (i) intracellular Gag-p6-ALIX binding is dependent on the presence of the LYPX motif in Gag-p6 and that this interaction can be modulated by the presence of CCL2 in the medium of HIV-infected cells; and (ii) HIV-1C Gag-p6 is unable to bind to ALIX irrespective of CCL2 addition or depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: Intracellular Gag-p6-ALIX interaction can be modulated by the presence of CCL2 in the medium of HIV-infected cells.
source: These results indicate that: (i) intracellular Gag-p6-ALIX binding is dependent on the presence of the LYPX motif in Gag-p6 and that this interaction can be modulated by the presence of CCL2 in the medium of HIV-infected cells; and (ii) HIV-1C Gag-p6 is unable to bind to ALIX irrespective of CCL2 addition or depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: HIV-1C Gag-p6 is unable to bind to ALIX irrespective of CCL2 addition or depletion.
source: These results indicate that: (i) intracellular Gag-p6-ALIX binding is dependent on the presence of the LYPX motif in Gag-p6 and that this interaction can be modulated by the presence of CCL2 in the medium of HIV-infected cells; and (ii) HIV-1C Gag-p6 is unable to bind to ALIX irrespective of CCL2 addition or depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: CCL2 significantly reorganizes the actin cytoskeleton in microglia.
source: It is known that CCL2 significantly reorganizes the actin cytoskeleton in microglia (Cross and Woodroofe, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: ALIX is intimately involved in actin rearrangement and polymerization in fibroblasts by directly interacting with F-actin through both the Bro1 and the proline-rich domains.
source: ALIX is also intimately involved in actin rearrangement and polymerization in fibroblasts by directly interacting with F-actin through both the Bro1 and the proline-rich domains (Pan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: ALIX knockdown affects both the cellular levels and distribution of F-actin.
source: Furthermore, ALIX knockdown affects both the cellular levels and distribution of F-actin (Bongiovanni et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: When CCL2 was immunodepleted (α-CCL2 treatment), ALIX was strictly associated with F-actin stress fibers in HeLa cells.
source: In HeLa cells, our results indicated that when CCL2 was immunodepleted (α-CCL2 treatment), ALIX was strictly associated with F-actin stress fibers (Figure 6A, 'α-CCL2' row - compare ALIX, Actin and Merged panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In CCL2-treated samples (including untreated cells, which contain endogenous CCL2, or cells treated with exogenous CCL2), ALIX was not associated with F-actin structures and was mostly distributed in the cytoplasm in HeLa cells.
source: In contrast, in CCL2-treated samples (including untreated cells, which contain endogenous CCL2, or cells treated with exogenous CCL2), ALIX was not associated with F-actin structures and was mostly distributed in the cytoplasm (Figure 6A, 'CCL2' row - compare ALIX, Actin and Merged panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In untreated and CCL2 treated macrophages, ALIX was diffusely distributed throughout the cell and was not associated with the large punctate podosomes containing F-actin.
source: Although the ALIX distribution in untreated and CCL2 treated macrophages appeared more punctate than in HeLa cells, it was diffusely distributed throughout the cell and was not associated with the large punctate podosomes containing F-actin (Figure 7A, 'Untreated' and 'CCL2' rows – compare ALIX, Actin and Merged panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Upon CCL2 depletion in macrophages, ALIX completely colocalized with F-actin in podosome structures.
source: In contrast, upon CCL2 depletion, ALIX completely colocalized with F-actin in podosome structures (Figure 7A, 'α-CCL2' row - compare ALIX, Actin and Merged panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Pearson coefficient is highest when the cells were treated with α-CCL2 antibodies.
source: We found that the Pearson coefficient is highest when the cells were treated with α-CCL2 antibodies, indicating that in the absence of CCL2, ALIX is associated with actin cytoskeletal structures in the cytoplasmic compartment, while at basal level and increased CCL2 levels, it is maintained in the cytoplasm away from actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 7B.

claim: In the absence of CCL2, ALIX is associated with actin cytoskeletal structures in the cytoplasmic compartment.
source: We found that the Pearson coefficient is highest when the cells were treated with α-CCL2 antibodies, indicating that in the absence of CCL2, ALIX is associated with actin cytoskeletal structures in the cytoplasmic compartment, while at basal level and increased CCL2 levels, it is maintained in the cytoplasm away from actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 7B.

claim: At basal level and increased CCL2 levels, ALIX is maintained in the cytoplasm away from actin cytoskeleton.
source: We found that the Pearson coefficient is highest when the cells were treated with α-CCL2 antibodies, indicating that in the absence of CCL2, ALIX is associated with actin cytoskeletal structures in the cytoplasmic compartment, while at basal level and increased CCL2 levels, it is maintained in the cytoplasm away from actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 7B.

claim: When the cells were treated with Latrunculin A, the amount of ALIX found in the soluble and insoluble fractions with all the treatments remained same.
source: Interestingly, when the cells were treated with Lantrunculin A, the amount of ALIX found in the soluble and insoluble fractions with all the treatments remained same, consistent with the idea that disruption of actin cytoskeleton by Lantrunculin A allows ALIX to be released (Figure 5B, middle and lower panel, lanes 5–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Disruption of actin cytoskeleton by Latrunculin A allows ALIX to be released.
source: Interestingly, when the cells were treated with Lantrunculin A, the amount of ALIX found in the soluble and insoluble fractions with all the treatments remained same, consistent with the idea that disruption of actin cytoskeleton by Lantrunculin A allows ALIX to be released (Figure 5B, middle and lower panel, lanes 5–8).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CCL2 regulates the redistribution of ALIX by releasing it from actin cytoskeleton.
source: Our results, for the first time, indicated that CCL2 regulates the redistribution of ALIX by releasing it from actin cytoskeleton, which in turn increases the levels of cytoplasmic ALIX accessible to Gag-p6 for binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5, Figure 6, and Figure 7.

claim: CCL2 increases the levels of cytoplasmic ALIX accessible to Gag-p6 for binding.
source: Our results, for the first time, indicated that CCL2 regulates the redistribution of ALIX by releasing it from actin cytoskeleton, which in turn increases the levels of cytoplasmic ALIX accessible to Gag-p6 for binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The typical Gag distribution indicative of accumulation of Gag near the plasma membrane was absent in HIV-1 producing HeLa cells treated with α-CCL2 antibodies.
source: This typical distribution was absent in HIV-1 producing HeLa cells treated with α-CCL2 antibodies (see Figure 8A 'α-CCL2' panels and Figure 8B), which showed a more even distribution of Gag pixel intensities throughout the cytosol (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Gag does not traffic to the plasma membrane and instead, is distributed throughout the cytoplasm in the absence of CCL2 and when ALIX is bound to actin cytoskeleton.
source: These results suggested that Gag does not traffic to the plasma membrane and instead, is distributed thoughout the cytoplasm in the absence of CCL2 and when ALIX is bound to actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the α-CCL2-treated cells, only a few virions at the cell surface of a small number of cells (14%) was observed.
source: In the α-CCL2-treated cells, however, only a few virions at the cell surface of a small number of cells (14%) was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The majority of α-CCL2-treated cells showed no virus particles on the cell surface but instead displayed virus-like particles in intracytoplasmic vacuoles.
source: The majority of cells showed no virus particles on the cell surface but instead displayed virus-like particles in intracytoplasmic vacuoles.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: In ~35% of the α-CCL2-treated cases, virus-like particles (~100 nm) inside vacuoles including those that are still attached to membrane and in early stages of Gag assembly were observed.
source: In ~35% of the cases, we observed what appear to be virus-like particles (~100 nm) inside vacuoles including those that are still attached to membrane and in early stages of Gag assembly (Figure 9A, second row, α-CCL2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In ~50% of the α-CCL2-treated cases, sub-viral-like electron dense particles (~30–40 nm) within intracytoplasmic vacuoles were observed.
source: In others (~50%), we observed sub-viral-like electron dense particles (~30–40 nm) (Figure 9A, third row, α-CCL2) also within intracytoplasmic vacuoles.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The unavailability of ALIX leads to perturbation of Gag trafficking.
source: These results indicated that the unavailability of ALIX leads to perturbation of Gag trafficking and that there is an accumulation of virus-like particles in intracellular vacuoles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The unavailability of ALIX leads to accumulation of virus-like particles in intracellular vacuoles.
source: These results indicated that the unavailability of ALIX leads to perturbation of Gag trafficking and that there is an accumulation of virus-like particles in intracellular vacuoles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: HIV-1IndieC1 is the least fit and HIV-1BADA is the most fit of the three viruses (HIV-1BADA, HIV-1CIndieC1, HIV-1IndieC+LY).
source: Our results showed that HIV-1IndieC1 is the least fit and HIV-1BADA is the most fit of the three viruses and that the insertion of the LY dipeptide in HIV-1C Gag-p6 enhances its replication in both cell types (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The insertion of the LY dipeptide in HIV-1C Gag-p6 enhances its replication in both PBMCs and MDMs.
source: Our results showed that HIV-1IndieC1 is the least fit and HIV-1BADA is the most fit of the three viruses and that the insertion of the LY dipeptide in HIV-1C Gag-p6 enhances its replication in both cell types (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Variants of HIV-1C that emerged in anti-retroviral therapy failure have been reported in India.
source: Variants of HIV-1C that emerged in anti-retroviral therapy failure have been reported in India and they also appear to dominate in Ethiopian HIV-1C isolates in the general HIV-1 infected population (Neogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Variants of HIV-1C with PYxE insertions appear to dominate in Ethiopian HIV-1C isolates in the general HIV-1 infected population.
source: Variants of HIV-1C that emerged in anti-retroviral therapy failure have been reported in India and they also appear to dominate in Ethiopian HIV-1C isolates in the general HIV-1 infected population (Neogi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: PYxE insertions were specific to HIV-1C as they were absent in other clades of HIV-1 or circulating recombinant forms (CRFs).
source: These insertions were specific to HIV-1C as they were absent in other clades of HIV-1 or circulating recombinant forms (CRFs).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: HIV-1C p6 with either PYRE or the PYKE exhibited strong binding to ALIX.
source: Interestingly, HIV-1C p6 with either PYRE or the PYKE exhibited strong binding to ALIX indicating that these insertions restored HIV-1Cp6-ALIX interaction (Figure 11A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: PYRE or PYKE insertions restored HIV-1Cp6-ALIX interaction.
source: Interestingly, HIV-1C p6 with either PYRE or the PYKE exhibited strong binding to ALIX indicating that these insertions restored HIV-1Cp6-ALIX interaction (Figure 11A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: All three insertions (LY, PYKE, PYRE) led to improved replication capacity compared to HIV-1C wild type.
source: As our results show, HIV-1C was the least replication competent virus, while HIV-1B was the most replication competent (Figure 11B). All three insertions led to improved replication capacity, and generally conferred a greater replication capacity when compared to HIV-1C wild type (Figure 11B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: PYxEi HIV-1C viruses display increased replication rates compared to HIV-1C wild-type virus.
source: Our results are consistent with reports showing that PYxEi HIV-1C viruses display increased replication rates compared to HIV-1C wild-type virus (Aralaguppe et al., 2017; Chaturbhuj et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature and experimental data in Figure 11B.

claim: HIV-1B displayed a higher degree of virus release compared to HIV-1C.
source: As shown in Figure 11C, HIV-1B displayed a higher degree of virus release (greater levels of Gag (p24) in the sucrose cushion pelleted virus preparation than in the cell lysate (pr55)), compared to HIV-1C (lower levels of Gag (p24) in the sucrose cushion pelleted virus preparation and an increased level of Gag (pr55) in the cell lysate).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The virus release deficit of HIV-1C was corrected with the insertion of LY, PYKE or PYRE.
source: Interestingly, this deficit was corrected with the insertion of LY, PYKE or PYRE into HIV-1C (Figure 11C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The improved replication competence of HIV-1C PYxE insertion variants is due to improved virion release owing to the acquisition of ALIX-binding capacity.
source: We conclude that the improved replication competence of HIV-1C PYxE insertion variants is due to improved virion release owing to the acquisition of ALIX-binding capacity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 11.

claim: The replication of all viruses with the ability to bind ALIX were reduced in the absence of ALIX.
source: The replication of all viruses with the ability to bind ALIX, namely HIV-1BADA, HIV-1CIndieC1+LY, HIV-1CIndieC1+PYRE and HIV-1CIndieC1+PYKE viruses, were reduced in the absence of ALIX (Figure 12B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Replication of viruses lacking the LY dipeptide were unaffected by ALIX silencing.
source: However, replication of viruses lacking the LY dipeptide, which are not dependent on ALIX for virus budding (e.g. HIV-1CIndieC1 and HIV-1BADA-ΔLY), were unaffected by ALIX silencing – although their replication was about 20–25% lower than HIV-1BADA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 12B.

claim: The PYxE insertion facilitated ALIX-binding and increased virus replication via enhanced particle release.
source: These results confirmed that the PYxE insertion not only facilitated ALIX-binding, but also increased virus replication via enhanced particle release that was made possible by the presence of a functional second late motif or its equivalent.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 12.

claim: Viruses with an intact LYPX motif or the PYxE insertion were inhibited by the expression of ALIX-DN.
source: We found that viruses with an intact LYPX motif or the PYxE insertion were inhibited by the expression of ALIX-DN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 12C.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type ALIX stimulated virus production in viruses with LYPX or PYxE motif.
source: In contrast, overexpression of wild-type ALIX stimulated virus production in viruses with LYPX or PYxE motif.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 12C.

claim: Viruses without an LY such as HIV-1CIndieC1, were unaffected by either the ALIX-DN or ALIX-WT expression.
source: Notably, viruses without an LY such as HIV-1CIndieC1, were unaffected by either the ALIX-DN or ALIX-WT expression (Figure 12C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Unlike the parent HIV-1C viruses lacking LY motif, PYxEi viruses had regained CCL2-responsiveness.
source: We found that, unlike the parent HIV-1C viruses lacking LY motif, PYxEi viruses had regained CCL2-responsiveness (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Control viruses with deletion of LY in HIV-1BADA were unresponsive to CCL2.
source: Control viruses with deletion of LY in HIV-1BADA were unresponsive to CCL2, while LY insertion in HIV-1C restored CCL2 responsiveness (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: LY insertion in HIV-1C restored CCL2 responsiveness.
source: Control viruses with deletion of LY in HIV-1BADA were unresponsive to CCL2, while LY insertion in HIV-1C restored CCL2 responsiveness (Figure 13).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The presence of LY or PYxE insertions improved virus replication due to improved particle release due to restoration of ALIX binding and thus responsiveness to CCL2.
source: These results together indicate that the presence of LY or PYxE insertions improved virus replication due to improved particle release due to restoration of ALIX binding and thus responsiveness to CCL2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data in Figure 13 and other figures.
